claim: De novo mutations in voltage- and ligand-gated channels have been associated with an increasing number of cases of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies.
source: De novo mutations in voltage- and ligand-gated channels have been associated with an increasing number of cases of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, which often fail to respond to classic antiseizure medications.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific knowledge and literature.

claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies often fail to respond to classic antiseizure medications.
source: De novo mutations in voltage- and ligand-gated channels have been associated with an increasing number of cases of developmental and epileptic encephalopathies, which often fail to respond to classic antiseizure medications.
evidence: This statement is based on established clinical knowledge about DEE treatment challenges.

claim: Two knock-in mouse models were examined that replicate de novo sequence variations in the human HCN1 voltage-gated channel gene: p.G391D and p.M153I.
source: Here, we examine two knock-in mouse models replicating de novo sequence variations in the human HCN1 voltage-gated channel gene, p.G391D and p.M153I (Hcn1G380D/+ and Hcn1M142I/+ in mouse), associated with severe drug-resistant neonatal- and childhood-onset epilepsy, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental models created and studied in this manuscript.

claim: The human HCN1 variants p.G391D and p.M153I are associated with severe drug-resistant neonatal- and childhood-onset epilepsy, respectively.
source: Here, we examine two knock-in mouse models replicating de novo sequence variations in the human HCN1 voltage-gated channel gene, p.G391D and p.M153I (Hcn1G380D/+ and Hcn1M142I/+ in mouse), associated with severe drug-resistant neonatal- and childhood-onset epilepsy, respectively.
evidence: This statement references clinical observations from patients with these variants, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Heterozygous mice from both Hcn1G380D/+ and Hcn1M142I/+ lines displayed spontaneous generalized tonic–clonic seizures.
source: Heterozygous mice from both lines displayed spontaneous generalized tonic–clonic seizures.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental observations reported in the manuscript, supported by ECoG recordings and behavioral observations.

claim: Animals replicating the p.G391D variant had an overall more severe phenotype than those with the p.M153I variant.
source: Animals replicating the p.G391D variant had an overall more severe phenotype, with pronounced alterations in the levels and distribution of HCN1 protein, including disrupted targeting to the axon terminals of basket cell interneurons.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Hcn1G380D/+ animals showed pronounced alterations in the levels and distribution of HCN1 protein.
source: Animals replicating the p.G391D variant had an overall more severe phenotype, with pronounced alterations in the levels and distribution of HCN1 protein, including disrupted targeting to the axon terminals of basket cell interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hcn1G380D/+ animals showed disrupted targeting of HCN1 protein to the axon terminals of basket cell interneurons.
source: Animals replicating the p.G391D variant had an overall more severe phenotype, with pronounced alterations in the levels and distribution of HCN1 protein, including disrupted targeting to the axon terminals of basket cell interneurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data showing loss of HCN1 labeling in basket cell terminals.

claim: Administration of the antiepileptic Na+ channel antagonists lamotrigine and phenytoin resulted in the paradoxical induction of seizures in both Hcn1G380D/+ and Hcn1M142I/+ mouse lines.
source: In line with clinical reports from patients with pathogenic HCN1 sequence variations, administration of the antiepileptic Na+ channel antagonists lamotrigine and phenytoin resulted in the paradoxical induction of seizures in both mouse lines, consistent with an impairment in inhibitory neuron function.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from drug challenge experiments.

claim: The paradoxical seizure induction by lamotrigine and phenytoin in the mouse models is consistent with clinical reports from patients with pathogenic HCN1 sequence variations.
source: In line with clinical reports from patients with pathogenic HCN1 sequence variations, administration of the antiepileptic Na+ channel antagonists lamotrigine and phenytoin resulted in the paradoxical induction of seizures in both mouse lines, consistent with an impairment in inhibitory neuron function.
evidence: This connects the mouse model findings to clinical observations, supported by citations.

claim: The paradoxical response to Na+ channel antagonists is consistent with an impairment in inhibitory neuron function.
source: In line with clinical reports from patients with pathogenic HCN1 sequence variations, administration of the antiepileptic Na+ channel antagonists lamotrigine and phenytoin resulted in the paradoxical induction of seizures in both mouse lines, consistent with an impairment in inhibitory neuron function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings based on known mechanisms.

claim: The HCN1 variants can render HCN1 channels unresponsive to classic antagonists.
source: We also show that these variants can render HCN1 channels unresponsive to classic antagonists, indicating the need to screen mutated channels to identify novel compounds with diverse mechanism of action.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced efficacy of ZD7288 on mutant channels.

claim: There is a need to screen mutated HCN1 channels to identify novel compounds with diverse mechanisms of action.
source: We also show that these variants can render HCN1 channels unresponsive to classic antagonists, indicating the need to screen mutated channels to identify novel compounds with diverse mechanism of action.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental findings about drug resistance.

claim: Approximately 30% of DEE patients carry at least one pathogenic variant in the top 100 known gene candidates for the disease.
source: Current estimates indicate that ~30% of DEE patients carry at least one pathogenic variant in the top 100 known gene candidates for the disease, with about a third of the affected genes falling into the category of voltage- and ligand-gated ion channels (Noebels, 2017; Oyrer et al., 2018; Wang and Frankel, 2021).
evidence: This is a statistical estimate from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: About a third of the genes associated with DEE fall into the category of voltage- and ligand-gated ion channels.
source: Current estimates indicate that ~30% of DEE patients carry at least one pathogenic variant in the top 100 known gene candidates for the disease, with about a third of the affected genes falling into the category of voltage- and ligand-gated ion channels (Noebels, 2017; Oyrer et al., 2018; Wang and Frankel, 2021).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: A total of 40 different missense variants in the HCN1 gene have been reported in patients affected by epilepsy and/or neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: To date, a total of 40 different missense variants in the HCN1 gene have been reported in patients affected by epilepsy and/or neurodevelopmental disorders (source: HGMD Professional 2020.4).
evidence: This is a count from a database of genetic mutations.

claim: At least 12 different de novo HCN1 variants have been linked to DEE.
source: Among these, at least 12 different de novo HCN1 variants have been linked to DEE (Nava et al., 2014; Butler et al., 2017; Marini et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a count from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: In pyramidal neurons, HCN1 channels are targeted to the distal portion of the apical dendrites.
source: In excitatory (pyramidal) neurons, the channel is targeted to the distal portion of the apical dendrites, where it constrains the dendritic integration of excitatory postsynaptic potentials, limiting excitability (Tsay et al., 2007; George et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an established finding about HCN1 localization, supported by citations.

claim: In pyramidal neurons, HCN1 channels constrain the dendritic integration of excitatory postsynaptic potentials, limiting excitability.
source: In excitatory (pyramidal) neurons, the channel is targeted to the distal portion of the apical dendrites, where it constrains the dendritic integration of excitatory postsynaptic potentials, limiting excitability (Tsay et al., 2007; George et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an established functional role of HCN1 channels, supported by citations.

claim: In PV+ interneurons, HCN1 channels are localized exclusively to axonal terminals.
source: In inhibitory (PV+) neurons, HCN1 channels are localized exclusively to axonal terminals, where they facilitate rapid action potential (AP) propagation (Roth and Hu, 2020) and may regulate GABA release (Southan et al., 2000; Aponte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an established finding about HCN1 localization in interneurons, supported by citations.

claim: In PV+ interneurons, HCN1 channels facilitate rapid action potential propagation.
source: In inhibitory (PV+) neurons, HCN1 channels are localized exclusively to axonal terminals, where they facilitate rapid action potential (AP) propagation (Roth and Hu, 2020) and may regulate GABA release (Southan et al., 2000; Aponte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an established functional role of HCN1 channels, supported by a citation.

claim: HCN1 channels in PV+ interneurons may regulate GABA release.
source: In inhibitory (PV+) neurons, HCN1 channels are localized exclusively to axonal terminals, where they facilitate rapid action potential (AP) propagation (Roth and Hu, 2020) and may regulate GABA release (Southan et al., 2000; Aponte et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a proposed functional role based on literature, indicated by 'may regulate', supported by citations.

claim: Decreased expression or activity of HCN1 channels has been posited to increase overall network excitability and contribute to epileptogenesis and seizures.
source: Decreased expression or activity of HCN1 channels, as observed in several rodent models of acquired epilepsy, has been thus posited to increase overall network excitability and contribute to epileptogenesis and seizures (Jung et al., 2011; McClelland et al., 2011; Brennan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: A prior attempt at modeling HCN1-linked DEE in mice resulted in a relatively mild phenotype where spontaneous seizures could not be systematically documented.
source: A prior attempt at modeling HCN1-linked DEE in mice (Bleakley et al., 2021) resulted in a relatively mild phenotype, wherein spontaneous seizures could not be systematically documented, despite the presence of epileptiform spikes on electrocorticogram recordings (ECoG).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: Mice with either global or forebrain-restricted deletion of HCN1 lack spontaneous seizures.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that mice with either global or forebrain-restricted deletion of HCN1 also lack spontaneous seizures (Nolan et al., 2003; Nolan et al., 2004), although seizure susceptibility is increased (Huang et al., 2009; Santoro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Mice with HCN1 deletion have increased seizure susceptibility.
source: Furthermore, it has been reported that mice with either global or forebrain-restricted deletion of HCN1 also lack spontaneous seizures (Nolan et al., 2003; Nolan et al., 2004), although seizure susceptibility is increased (Huang et al., 2009; Santoro et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The HCN1 variants c.1172G>A/p.Gly391Asp and c.459G>C/p.Met153Ile were selected based on three criteria: severity of disease, occurrence in at least two independent patients with similar epilepsy phenotypes, and differing biophysical effects on channel function.
source: We examined variants c.1172G>A/p.Gly391Asp and c.459G>C/p.Met153Ile based on three criteria: severity of disease; occurrence in at least two independent patients with similar epilepsy phenotypes; and differing biophysical effects on channel function when tested in heterologous expression systems (Marini et al., 2018).
evidence: This explains the rationale for selecting these specific variants for study.

claim: Clinical reports suggest that seizures in patients with HCN1 variants are poorly controlled with standard antiseizure medications.
source: Moreover, clinical reports suggest that seizures are poorly controlled with standard antiseizure medications and that certain anticonvulsants in fact exacerbate seizures in these patients (Marini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of clinical observations from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Certain anticonvulsants exacerbate seizures in patients with HCN1 variants.
source: Moreover, clinical reports suggest that seizures are poorly controlled with standard antiseizure medications and that certain anticonvulsants in fact exacerbate seizures in these patients (Marini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of clinical observations from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ mice had consistently smaller body weights at weaning in both sexes.
source: No overt differences were noted in pup development, except for consistently smaller body weights at weaning in Hcn1GD/+ mice of both sexes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: Smaller body weights persisted for the life of Hcn1GD/+ animals.
source: Smaller body weights persisted for the life of Hcn1GD/+ animals and were accompanied by an ~12% reduction in adult brain weight with gross brain anatomy otherwise normal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from longitudinal measurements, supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals showed an approximately 12% reduction in adult brain weight.
source: Smaller body weights persisted for the life of Hcn1GD/+ animals and were accompanied by an ~12% reduction in adult brain weight with gross brain anatomy otherwise normal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experiments, supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Gross brain anatomy was otherwise normal in Hcn1GD/+ animals despite reduced brain weight.
source: Smaller body weights persisted for the life of Hcn1GD/+ animals and were accompanied by an ~12% reduction in adult brain weight with gross brain anatomy otherwise normal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from histological analysis, supported by images in Figure 1B.

claim: Both cerebellum and brainstem areas were significantly smaller in Hcn1GD/+ mice compared to WT.
source: Thus, both cerebellum and brainstem areas were significantly smaller in Hcn1GD/+ mice compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with the cerebellum more affected than the brainstem, consistent with the higher expression of HCN1 protein in this region (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from brain sections, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cerebellum was more affected than the brainstem in Hcn1GD/+ mice.
source: Thus, both cerebellum and brainstem areas were significantly smaller in Hcn1GD/+ mice compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with the cerebellum more affected than the brainstem, consistent with the higher expression of HCN1 protein in this region (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from measurements, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The greater effect on cerebellum compared to brainstem in Hcn1GD/+ mice is consistent with the higher expression of HCN1 protein in the cerebellum.
source: Thus, both cerebellum and brainstem areas were significantly smaller in Hcn1GD/+ mice compared to WT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), with the cerebellum more affected than the brainstem, consistent with the higher expression of HCN1 protein in this region (Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the anatomical findings to known HCN1 expression patterns, supported by a citation.

claim: Reduced mean body weight was observed in Hcn1MI/+ males.
source: Reduced mean body weight was also observed in Hcn1MI/+ males, but no decrease in brain size was noted in either sex for this line (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from measurements, supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: No decrease in brain size was noted in either sex for the Hcn1MI/+ line.
source: Reduced mean body weight was also observed in Hcn1MI/+ males, but no decrease in brain size was noted in either sex for this line (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from measurements, supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: Both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed a significant number of premature deaths.
source: Survival curves revealed a significant number of premature deaths in both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct observation from survival monitoring, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Many animals were found dead in the cage without having shown prior signs of distress, suggesting sudden death.
source: In many instances, animals were found dead in the cage without having shown prior signs of distress, suggesting sudden death.
evidence: This is a direct observation from animal monitoring.

claim: Most deaths among Hcn1GD/+ animals occurred before the age of 3 months.
source: Most deaths among Hcn1GD/+ animals occurred before the age of 3 months (Figure 1C, left), with no difference between the sexes (survival rate at 30 weeks: 78% male versus 75% female Hcn1GD/+ mice, p=0.369, Fisher's exact probability test).
evidence: This is a temporal pattern observed in survival data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: There was no difference in survival between male and female Hcn1GD/+ mice.
source: Most deaths among Hcn1GD/+ animals occurred before the age of 3 months (Figure 1C, left), with no difference between the sexes (survival rate at 30 weeks: 78% male versus 75% female Hcn1GD/+ mice, p=0.369, Fisher's exact probability test).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of survival data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: For Hcn1MI/+ animals, females were more severely affected than males in terms of survival.
source: In contrast, for Hcn1MI/+ animals, females were more severely affected than males (survival rate at 30 weeks: 86% male versus 55% female Hcn1MI/+ mice, p<0.001, Fisher's exact probability test), with most deaths in either sex occurring at an age greater than 3 months (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of survival data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Most deaths in Hcn1MI/+ animals occurred at an age greater than 3 months.
source: In contrast, for Hcn1MI/+ animals, females were more severely affected than males (survival rate at 30 weeks: 86% male versus 55% female Hcn1MI/+ mice, p<0.001, Fisher's exact probability test), with most deaths in either sex occurring at an age greater than 3 months (Figure 1C, right).
evidence: This is a temporal pattern observed in survival data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed locomotor hyperactivity in the open field.
source: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed locomotor hyperactivity in the open field, with significant increases in distance moved and running speed, but a reduction in the center versus border zone occupancy ratio, potentially indicative of increased anxiety-like behavior in both lines (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed significant increases in distance moved and running speed in the open field.
source: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed locomotor hyperactivity in the open field, with significant increases in distance moved and running speed, but a reduction in the center versus border zone occupancy ratio, potentially indicative of increased anxiety-like behavior in both lines (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed a reduction in the center versus border zone occupancy ratio in the open field, potentially indicative of increased anxiety-like behavior.
source: Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals showed locomotor hyperactivity in the open field, with significant increases in distance moved and running speed, but a reduction in the center versus border zone occupancy ratio, potentially indicative of increased anxiety-like behavior in both lines (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral testing with an interpretation, supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals displayed significant changes in the base of support (BOS), with the front paws' BOS being wider at both speed ranges.
source: When runs of similar speed were compared, significant changes in the base of support (BOS) were observed in Hcn1GD/+ animals, with the front paws' BOS being wider at both speed ranges (Figure 2F), and the hind paws' BOS narrower at higher running speeds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from gait analysis, supported by data in Figure 2F.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals showed narrower hind paws' BOS at higher running speeds.
source: When runs of similar speed were compared, significant changes in the base of support (BOS) were observed in Hcn1GD/+ animals, with the front paws' BOS being wider at both speed ranges (Figure 2F), and the hind paws' BOS narrower at higher running speeds (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from gait analysis, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No BOS alterations were noted in Hcn1MI/+ animals.
source: No BOS alterations were noted in Hcn1MI/+ animals or any of the other gait parameters measured (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a negative finding from gait analysis, supported by data in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals displayed significant difficulties in climbing down a vertical pole.
source: When comparing the ability to climb down a vertical pole, Hcn1GD/+ animals displayed significant difficulties, with only 1 of 18 animals able to successfully complete the test during trials 1 and 2, and 2 of 18 animals succeeding in trial 3 (Figure 2H, Figure 2—video 1 and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from motor coordination testing, supported by data in Figure 2H.

claim: Hcn1MI/+ animals performed as well as their WT littermates in the pole test.
source: In contrast, Hcn1MI/+ animals performed as well as their WT littermates, with all mice successfully completing the task and their average latencies to reach the floor comparable between the two groups (Figure 2I, Figure 2—video 3, Figure 2—video 4).
evidence: This is a direct observation from motor coordination testing, supported by data in Figure 2I.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals failed to display normal alternation behavior in the Y maze, with alternation rates not exceeding the chance level of 50%.
source: When tested in a Y maze-based spontaneous alternation task (Figure 3A), Hcn1GD/+ animals failed to display normal alternation behavior, with alternation rates not exceeding the chance level of 50% (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: Hcn1MI/+ animals showed equal performance compared to WT littermates in the Y maze spontaneous alternation task.
source: In contrast, Hcn1MI/+ animals showed equal performance compared to WT littermates.
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, with data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals needed significantly less time to complete the required 24 arm transitions in the Y maze.
source: Both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals needed significantly less time to complete the required 24 arm transitions (Figure 3C), consistent with the locomotor hyperactivity observed in these mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutant mice from both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ lines were able to distinguish the novel object from the familiar object in the object recognition memory task.
source: We found that mutant mice from both lines were able to distinguish the novel object from the familiar object, as reflected in positive discrimination indices (D.I.) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from behavioral testing, supported by data in Figure 3E.

claim: Hcn1GD/+ animals spent a significantly higher time exploring the novel object compared to their WT littermates.
source: Hcn1GD/+ animals also spent a significantly higher time exploring the novel object, compared to their WT littermates, although the meaning of this finding is unclear.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from behavioral testing, with data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Adult mice from both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ lines and sexes displayed spontaneous GTCSs with distinct electrographic signature on ECoG traces.
source: Adult mice from both lines and sexes were found to display spontaneous GTCSs with distinct electrographic signature on ECoG traces (Figure 4A and C) and behavioral manifestation on video recordings (Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from ECoG recordings and video observations, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Seizure events were comparatively infrequent, ranging from 0.6 to 4.1 seizures per week in Hcn1GD/+ mice.
source: Seizure events were comparatively infrequent, ranging from 0.6 to 4.1 seizures per week in Hcn1GD/+ mice (with 2/8 individuals failing to show seizures during the time recorded) and from 0.6 to 5.1 seizures per week in Hcn1MI/+ mice (with 2/12 individuals displaying no seizures during the recorded period).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of seizure frequency from ECoG recordings.

claim: 2 out of 8 Hcn1GD/+ individuals failed to show seizures during the recording period.
source: Seizure events were comparatively infrequent, ranging from 0.6 to 4.1 seizures per week in Hcn1GD/+ mice (with 2/8 individuals failing to show seizures during the time recorded) and from 0.6 to 5.1 seizures per week in Hcn1MI/+ mice (with 2/12 individuals displaying no seizures during the recorded period).
evidence: This is a direct observation from ECoG recordings.

claim: Seizure events ranged from 0.6 to 5.1 seizures per week in Hcn1MI/+ mice.
source: Seizure events were comparatively infrequent, ranging from 0.6 to 4.1 seizures per week in Hcn1GD/+ mice (with 2/8 individuals failing to show seizures during the time recorded) and from 0.6 to 5.1 seizures per week in Hcn1MI/+ mice (with 2/12 individuals displaying no seizures during the recorded period).
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of seizure frequency from ECoG recordings.

claim: 2 out of 12 Hcn1MI/+ individuals displayed no seizures during the recorded period.
source: Seizure events were comparatively infrequent, ranging from 0.6 to 4.1 seizures per week in Hcn1GD/+ mice (with 2/8 individuals failing to show seizures during the time recorded) and from 0.6 to 5.1 seizures per week in Hcn1MI/+ mice (with 2/12 individuals displaying no seizures during the recorded period).
evidence: This is a direct observation from ECoG recordings.

claim: Animals from the Hcn1GD/+ line had on average lower maximum grade seizures compared to Hcn1MI/+ animals.
source: Despite the overall more severe phenotype of Hcn1GD/+ animals, based on body weight, brain size, behavioral performance, and general appearance, when rated on a modified Racine scale (see 'Materials and methods') we found that animals from the Hcn1GD/+ line had on average lower maximum grade seizures compared to Hcn1MI/+ animals (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from seizure grading, supported by data in Figure 4B and D.

claim: Upregulation of neuropeptide Y in dentate gyrus mossy fibers was observed in mutant animals from both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ lines.
source: In line with our video ECoG findings, we observed upregulation of neuropeptide Y in dentate gyrus mossy fibers, alterations in granule cell layer morphology and extracellular matrix deposition in the dentate gyrus, as well as increased hippocampal gliosis in a majority of mutant animals from both lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Alterations in granule cell layer morphology and extracellular matrix deposition in the dentate gyrus were observed in mutant animals from both lines.
source: In line with our video ECoG findings, we observed upregulation of neuropeptide Y in dentate gyrus mossy fibers, alterations in granule cell layer morphology and extracellular matrix deposition in the dentate gyrus, as well as increased hippocampal gliosis in a majority of mutant animals from both lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from histological analysis, supported by images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increased hippocampal gliosis was observed in a majority of mutant animals from both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ lines.
source: In line with our video ECoG findings, we observed upregulation of neuropeptide Y in dentate gyrus mossy fibers, alterations in granule cell layer morphology and extracellular matrix deposition in the dentate gyrus, as well as increased hippocampal gliosis in a majority of mutant animals from both lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The hippocampal markers observed are consistent with the presence of spontaneous seizures and altered excitability within the hippocampal circuit.
source: Such findings are consistent with the presence of spontaneous seizures and altered excitability within the hippocampal circuit (Houser, 1990; Marksteiner et al., 1990; Stringer, 1996; Magagna-Poveda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the histological findings based on literature, supported by citations.

claim: The HCN1-G391D mutation causes channels to fail to express current on their own.
source: HCN1 subunits with the G391D mutation fail to express current on their own, but when combined with WT subunits (as occurs in patients and heterozygote Hcn1GD/+ mice) yield, in the ~20% fraction of cells that show measurable currents, a 'leaky' channel with significantly decreased current density but a greatly increased voltage- and time-independent inward, depolarizing current component.
evidence: This is a summary of prior in vitro findings from heterologous expression systems, supported by a citation.

claim: When HCN1-G391D subunits are combined with WT subunits, approximately 20% of cells show measurable currents.
source: HCN1 subunits with the G391D mutation fail to express current on their own, but when combined with WT subunits (as occurs in patients and heterozygote Hcn1GD/+ mice) yield, in the ~20% fraction of cells that show measurable currents, a 'leaky' channel with significantly decreased current density but a greatly increased voltage- and time-independent inward, depolarizing current component.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from prior in vitro studies, supported by a citation.

claim: HCN1-G391D/WT heteromeric channels show significantly decreased current density but a greatly increased voltage- and time-independent inward, depolarizing current component.
source: HCN1 subunits with the G391D mutation fail to express current on their own, but when combined with WT subunits (as occurs in patients and heterozygote Hcn1GD/+ mice) yield, in the ~20% fraction of cells that show measurable currents, a 'leaky' channel with significantly decreased current density but a greatly increased voltage- and time-independent inward, depolarizing current component.
evidence: This is a summary of biophysical properties from prior in vitro studies, supported by a citation.

claim: The M153I mutation slightly reduces current density but accelerates the opening kinetics and shifts the voltage dependence of the HCN1 channel to more depolarized potentials.
source: In contrast, the M153I mutation only slightly reduces current density, but accelerates the opening kinetics and shifts the voltage dependence of the HCN1 channel to more depolarized potentials (midpoint of activation is shifted by +36 mV for homomeric mutant channels and by +12 mV for heteromeric M153I/WT channels).
evidence: This is a summary of biophysical properties from prior in vitro studies, supported by a citation.

claim: The midpoint of activation is shifted by +36 mV for homomeric M153I mutant channels and by +12 mV for heteromeric M153I/WT channels.
source: In contrast, the M153I mutation only slightly reduces current density, but accelerates the opening kinetics and shifts the voltage dependence of the HCN1 channel to more depolarized potentials (midpoint of activation is shifted by +36 mV for homomeric mutant channels and by +12 mV for heteromeric M153I/WT channels).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from prior in vitro studies, supported by a citation.

claim: HCN1 antibody labeling showed a substantial decrease in overall HCN1 protein levels in Hcn1GD/+ brains.
source: This gradient of expression was preserved in brains from both lines, although labeling revealed a substantial decrease in overall HCN1 protein levels in Hcn1GD/+ brains, with a smaller but still significant decrease observed in Hcn1MI/+ brains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: A smaller but still significant decrease in HCN1 protein levels was observed in Hcn1MI/+ brains.
source: This gradient of expression was preserved in brains from both lines, although labeling revealed a substantial decrease in overall HCN1 protein levels in Hcn1GD/+ brains, with a smaller but still significant decrease observed in Hcn1MI/+ brains (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: The voltage sag was absent in Hcn1GD/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: In whole-cell patch-clamp recordings, such results were matched by a substantial reduction in the voltage sag observed in response to hyperpolarizing current injections, a hallmark of Ih activity in neurons (Figure 5C and D). The voltage sag was absent in Hcn1GD/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons and significantly reduced in Hcn1MI/+.
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The voltage sag was significantly reduced in Hcn1MI/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: In whole-cell patch-clamp recordings, such results were matched by a substantial reduction in the voltage sag observed in response to hyperpolarizing current injections, a hallmark of Ih activity in neurons (Figure 5C and D). The voltage sag was absent in Hcn1GD/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons and significantly reduced in Hcn1MI/+.
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5C and D.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons of Hcn1GD/+ mice displayed a significant depolarization in the RMP.
source: Surprisingly, despite the loss of HCN1 protein expression, CA1 pyramidal neurons of Hcn1GD/+ mice displayed a significant depolarization in the RMP; in contrast, there was no change in RMP in Hcn1MI/+ neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: There was no change in RMP in Hcn1MI/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Surprisingly, despite the loss of HCN1 protein expression, CA1 pyramidal neurons of Hcn1GD/+ mice displayed a significant depolarization in the RMP; in contrast, there was no change in RMP in Hcn1MI/+ neurons (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5E.

claim: The more positive RMP of Hcn1GD/+ mice was unexpected considering the strong reduction in HCN1 protein expression and hyperpolarized RMP in mice lacking HCN1 channels.
source: The more positive RMP of Hcn1GD/+ mice was unexpected considering the strong reduction in HCN1 protein expression (Figure 5B) and hyperpolarized RMP in mice lacking HCN1 channels (Nolan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current findings to prior literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The depolarized RMP in Hcn1GD/+ neurons may reflect the depolarizing action of the increased voltage-independent 'leak' current seen with certain HCN1 channel mutations.
source: This may reflect the depolarizing action of the increased voltage-independent 'leak' current seen with certain HCN1 channel mutations, including p.G391D and p.M305L (Bleakley et al., 2021), and/or secondary changes in the function of other neuronal conductances.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Input resistance was unaltered in both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Input resistance was unaltered in both lines (GD: WT = 137.8 ± 7.1 MΩ, n = 20 cells, versus Hcn1GD/+ = 153.7 ± 7.8 MΩ, n = 21; MI: WT = 128.4 ± 9.5 MΩ, n = 25, versus Hcn1MI/+ = 125.5 ± 7.9 MΩ, n = 38).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: CA1 cells in both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ mouse lines show an impaired ability to fire APs.
source: The possibility that the expression of mutant HCN1 channels may cause secondary changes in CA1 pyramidal neuron function is consistent with our finding that CA1 cells in both mouse lines show an impaired ability to fire APs, a phenotype not observed with acute application of the HCN channel-specific blocker ZD7288 (Gasparini and DiFrancesco, 1997; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The impaired ability to fire APs in mutant CA1 neurons is not observed with acute application of the HCN channel-specific blocker ZD7288.
source: The possibility that the expression of mutant HCN1 channels may cause secondary changes in CA1 pyramidal neuron function is consistent with our finding that CA1 cells in both mouse lines show an impaired ability to fire APs, a phenotype not observed with acute application of the HCN channel-specific blocker ZD7288 (Gasparini and DiFrancesco, 1997; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: A majority of Hcn1GD/+ neurons (76%) showed a reduction in the number of APs fired during 1-s-long depolarizing current steps.
source: Thus, application of positive current steps from a common holding potential of –70 mV revealed an abnormal firing pattern in CA1 neurons from both lines (Figure 5C), wherein a majority of Hcn1GD/+ neurons and a significant fraction of Hcn1MI/+ neurons showed a reduction in the number of APs fired during 1-s-long depolarizing current steps (fraction of neurons with abnormal firing pattern: 16/21 cells = 76% Hcn1GD/+ versus 13/35 cells = 37% Hcn1MI/+, p=0.006, Fisher's exact probability test showing a larger effect in the former cohort; 1/44 cells = 2% in the combined set of WT littermate neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: A significant fraction of Hcn1MI/+ neurons (37%) showed a reduction in the number of APs fired during 1-s-long depolarizing current steps.
source: Thus, application of positive current steps from a common holding potential of –70 mV revealed an abnormal firing pattern in CA1 neurons from both lines (Figure 5C), wherein a majority of Hcn1GD/+ neurons and a significant fraction of Hcn1MI/+ neurons showed a reduction in the number of APs fired during 1-s-long depolarizing current steps (fraction of neurons with abnormal firing pattern: 16/21 cells = 76% Hcn1GD/+ versus 13/35 cells = 37% Hcn1MI/+, p=0.006, Fisher's exact probability test showing a larger effect in the former cohort; 1/44 cells = 2% in the combined set of WT littermate neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Only 2% of WT littermate neurons showed abnormal firing pattern.
source: Thus, application of positive current steps from a common holding potential of –70 mV revealed an abnormal firing pattern in CA1 neurons from both lines (Figure 5C), wherein a majority of Hcn1GD/+ neurons and a significant fraction of Hcn1MI/+ neurons showed a reduction in the number of APs fired during 1-s-long depolarizing current steps (fraction of neurons with abnormal firing pattern: 16/21 cells = 76% Hcn1GD/+ versus 13/35 cells = 37% Hcn1MI/+, p=0.006, Fisher's exact probability test showing a larger effect in the former cohort; 1/44 cells = 2% in the combined set of WT littermate neurons).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Rheobase was unaltered in both Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ CA1 pyramidal neurons when measured from a holding potential of –70 mV.
source: In contrast, rheobase was unaltered in both lines when measured from a holding potential of –70 mV (GD: WT = 100 ± 9.6 pA, n = 20, versus Hcn1GD/+ = 114.3 ± 8.0 pA, n = 21; MI: WT = 101.0 ± 6.8 pA, n = 25 versus Hcn1MI/+ = 98.6 ± 6.4 pA, n = 38), and no changes were observed in AP threshold, AP peak or AP width (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No changes were observed in AP threshold, AP peak or AP width in mutant CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: In contrast, rheobase was unaltered in both lines when measured from a holding potential of –70 mV (GD: WT = 100 ± 9.6 pA, n = 20, versus Hcn1GD/+ = 114.3 ± 8.0 pA, n = 21; MI: WT = 101.0 ± 6.8 pA, n = 25 versus Hcn1MI/+ = 98.6 ± 6.4 pA, n = 38), and no changes were observed in AP threshold, AP peak or AP width (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The findings suggest a lack of secondary changes in voltage-gated Na+ channel function in pyramidal neurons.
source: These findings suggest a lack of secondary changes in voltage-gated Na+ channel function, at least in pyramidal neurons, unlike what has been reported in the case of the p.M305L variant (Bleakley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiological findings, supported by a citation.

claim: A microarray-based gene expression screening from total hippocampal lysates did not reveal any changes in Na+ channel transcript levels.
source: A microarray-based gene expression screening from WT, Hcn1GD/+, and Hcn1MI/+ total hippocampal lysates also did not reveal any changes in Na+ channel transcript levels, similar to those observed in Bleakley et al., 2021 (Source data 1; the only candidate with a p-value<0.001 being a K+ channel), although alterations in protein levels or post-translational modulation cannot be ruled out by this approach.
evidence: This is a direct observation from gene expression analysis, with data in Source data 1.

claim: There was a complete loss of HCN1 protein staining in the cerebellar pinceau of Hcn1GD/+ animals.
source: Surprisingly, at this location, we found a complete loss of HCN1 protein staining in Hcn1GD/+ animals, while the distribution in Hcn1MI/+ appeared relatively normal (Figure 6, top row).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 6.

claim: The distribution of HCN1 protein in the cerebellar pinceau appeared relatively normal in Hcn1MI/+ animals.
source: Surprisingly, at this location, we found a complete loss of HCN1 protein staining in Hcn1GD/+ animals, while the distribution in Hcn1MI/+ appeared relatively normal (Figure 6, top row).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 6.

claim: The loss of HCN1 in the pinceau suggests that the mutation may exert a dominant negative effect by co-assembling with WT HCN1 subunits, resulting in improper trafficking and/or premature degradation.
source: This result is unexpected as levels of HCN1 protein expressed from the WT allele should be normal, providing at least a half dosage in Hcn1GD/+ cells, and suggests that the mutation may exert a dominant negative effect by co-assembling with WT HCN1 subunits, resulting in improper trafficking and/or premature degradation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunohistochemical findings.

claim: KV1.2 labeling of the pinceau was completely lost in Hcn1GD/+ but not Hcn1MI/+ brains.
source: As shown in Figure 6 (middle row), KV1.2 labeling of the pinceau was completely lost, similar to HCN1 protein labeling, in Hcn1GD/+ but not Hcn1MI/+ brains.
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 6.

claim: The downregulation of KV1.2 does not appear to be due to co-regulation with HCN1, as normal KV1.2 labeling is still present in the cerebellum of HCN1 knockout mice.
source: The downregulation of KV1.2 does not appear to be due to co-regulation with HCN1, as normal KV1.2 labeling is still present in the cerebellum of HCN1 knockout mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and the expression of the two channels at the cerebellar pinceau was shown to be independently regulated (Kole et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on observations in HCN1 knockout mice and literature, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: There was a complete loss of ATP1a3 labeling in Hcn1GD/+ but not Hcn1MI/+ animals compared to WT controls.
source: As shown in Figure 6 (bottom row), similar to HCN1 and KV1.2, there was a complete loss of ATP1a3 labeling in Hcn1GD/+ but not Hcn1MI/+ animals compared to WT controls.
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 6.

claim: Immunolabeling of HCN1 protein in the axon terminals of hippocampal PV+ interneurons was strongly reduced in Hcn1GD/+ animals, although not completely absent.
source: Similar to what was observed in the apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 5A and B), immunolabeling of HCN1 protein in the axon terminals of hippocampal PV+ interneurons was strongly reduced in Hcn1GD/+ animals, although not completely absent (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis, supported by images in Figure 7A.

claim: Following injection of either HA-HCN1-WT or HA-HCN1-MI, staining with anti-HA antibodies revealed efficient targeting and expression of virus-driven protein in the axonal terminals of PV+ interneurons.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, following injection of either HA-HCN1-WT or HA-HCN1-MI, staining with anti-HA antibodies revealed efficient targeting and expression of virus-driven protein in the axonal terminals of PV+ interneurons.
evidence: This is a direct observation from viral transduction experiments, supported by images in Figure 7B.

claim: Injection of HA-HCN1-GD did not result in detectable levels of HA-tagged protein in axonal terminals, while protein accumulation was observed in the soma of targeted neurons.
source: In stark contrast, injection of HA-HCN1-GD did not result in detectable levels of HA-tagged protein in axonal terminals, while protein accumulation was observed in the soma of targeted neurons (Figure 7B, top row).
evidence: This is a direct observation from viral transduction experiments, supported by images in Figure 7B.

claim: Co-staining with anti-parvalbumin antibodies revealed a striking decrease of axonal parvalbumin protein labeling in the targeted CA1 area from brains injected with virus expressing HA-HCN1-GD but not with virus expressing HA-HCN1-WT or HA-HCN1-MI.
source: Co-staining with anti-parvalbumin antibodies furthermore revealed a striking decrease of axonal parvalbumin protein labeling in the targeted CA1 area from brains injected with virus expressing HA-HCN1-GD but not with virus expressing HA-HCN1-WT or HA-HCN1-MI (Figure 7B, middle row, and Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunohistochemical analysis of virus-injected brains, supported by images in Figure 7B and supplements.

claim: Clinical reports from at least four different patients with HCN1-linked DEE consistently revealed worsening of seizures after administration of either lamotrigine or phenytoin.
source: Clinical reports from at least four different patients with HCN1-linked DEE (carrying variants p.M305L, p.G391D, and p.I380F; Marini et al., 2018; Bleakley et al., 2021; C. Marini, personal communication, March 2021) consistently revealed worsening of seizures after administration of either lamotrigine (LTG) or phenytoin.
evidence: This is a summary of clinical observations from multiple sources, supported by citations and personal communication.

claim: Two unrelated patients with the p.G391D variant had neonatal seizure onset, characterized by daily asymmetric tonic seizures with apnea and cyanosis, severe developmental delay, and died between 14 and 15 months of age.
source: A particularly striking example is provided by the p.G391D variant, identified in two unrelated patients with similar course of disease. Both patients had neonatal seizure onset, characterized by daily asymmetric tonic seizures with apnea and cyanosis, severe developmental delay, and died between 14 and 15 months of age.
evidence: This is a summary of clinical case reports.

claim: Both patients with the p.G391D variant showed a paradoxical response to phenytoin, which caused the induction of status epilepticus.
source: Both patients also showed a paradoxical response to phenytoin, which caused the induction of status epilepticus.
evidence: This is a summary of clinical observations from case reports.

claim: Administration of LTG (23 mg/kg, i.p.) induced convulsive seizures within 90 min from injection in 11/15 Hcn1GD/+ animals.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we found that administration of LTG (23 mg/kg, i.p.) induced convulsive seizures, defined as grade 3 or higher on a modified Racine scale (see 'Materials and Methods'), within 90 min from injection in 11/15 HCN1GD/+ animals (Figure 8A and C, left).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from drug challenge experiments, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: Convulsive seizures were observed in 6/9 Hcn1MI/+ mice in response to LTG.
source: Similar outcomes were seen in Hcn1MI/+ animals, where convulsive seizures were observed in 6/9 mice in response to LTG (Figure 8A and C, right).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from drug challenge experiments, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: 14/18 animals tested from the Hcn1GD/+ line developed convulsive seizures within 2.5 hr of phenytoin injection.
source: Results with phenytoin (30 mg/kg PE, i.p.) were even more striking as 14/18 animals tested from the Hcn1GD/+ line developed convulsive seizures within 2.5 hr of injection (this number includes 11/14 animals with no prior drug exposure and 3/4 animals previously exposed to LTG; Figure 8B and C, left).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from drug challenge experiments, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: 10/15 Hcn1MI/+ mice showed seizures following phenytoin injection.
source: Among Hcn1MI/+ animals, we observed seizures in 10/15 mice following phenytoin injection, with similar temporal pattern and ECoG signatures compared to Hcn1GD/+ mice (this number includes 6/8 animals without prior drug exposure and 4/7 animals previously exposed to LTG, Figure 8B and C, right).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from drug challenge experiments, supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: None of the Hcn1GD/+ or Hcn1MI/+ animals tested had convulsive seizures in response to vehicle injection during the period of observation.
source: All the Hcn1GD/+ or Hcn1MI/+ animals tested, either in response to LTG or phenytoin, were randomized to receive a control vehicle injection either 1 week before or 1 week after the drug administration session. None had convulsive seizures in response to vehicle injection during the period of observation (4 hr for behavioral experiments and 24 hr for video ECoG experiments), further confirming that the seizures observed in the period following drug administration were a direct consequence of the pharmacological challenge (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a control experiment result, supported by data in Figure 8C.

claim: Administration of sodium valproate (250 mg/kg, i.p.) did not result in the occurrence of convulsive seizures in any of the Hcn1GD/+ or Hcn1MI/+ animals tested.
source: As an additional control, we tested the effects of a third anticonvulsant, namely, sodium valproate (VPA), which has not been reported to worsen seizures in any of the patients with pathogenic HCN1 sequence variations in our database. Administration of sodium valproate (250 mg/kg, i.p.) did not result in the occurrence of convulsive seizures in any of the Hcn1GD/+ or Hcn1MI/+ animals tested (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a control experiment result, supported by data in Figure 8C.

claim: Use of 250 mg/kg VPA resulted in profound sedation of Hcn1GD/+ mice, which was not seen in Hcn1MI/+ mice or WT littermate controls.
source: However, use of 250 mg/kg VPA resulted in profound sedation of Hcn1GD/+ mice, which was not seen in Hcn1MI/+ mice or WT littermate controls, with 9/10 Hcn1GD/+ animals failing to respond to gentle touch or passive moving of the tail 45 min after drug injection versus 2/8 Hcn1MI/+ and 0/8 WT animals (note that tail pinching still elicited a response in all mice tested).
evidence: This is a direct observation from drug challenge experiments.

claim: LTG had no effects on either the midpoint voltage of activation or maximal tail current density of either HCN1 or HCN2 channels.
source: Surprisingly, we found that LTG had no effects on either the midpoint voltage of activation or maximal tail current density of either HCN1 or HCN2 channels; LTG also had no effects when HCN1 was coexpressed with its auxiliary subunit TRIP8b (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from heterologous expression experiments, supported by data in Figure 9B.

claim: LTG had no effects on HCN1 channels when coexpressed with the auxiliary subunit TRIP8b.
source: Surprisingly, we found that LTG had no effects on either the midpoint voltage of activation or maximal tail current density of either HCN1 or HCN2 channels; LTG also had no effects when HCN1 was coexpressed with its auxiliary subunit TRIP8b (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from heterologous expression experiments, supported by data in Figure 9B.

claim: LTG exerted its expected inhibitory effect on NaV1.5 sodium channel currents under the same conditions.
source: In contrast, under the same conditions, LTG exerted its expected inhibitory effect on NaV1.5 sodium channel currents (Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Qiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a control experiment result confirming LTG activity, supported by data in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claim: LTG is not a direct activator of HCN channels.
source: These results clearly show that LTG is not a direct activator of HCN channels and suggest that any effects reported in neurons are the result of indirect regulation of Ih, perhaps secondary to Na+ channel block, and likely contingent on cell-specific, state-dependent signal transduction pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Any effects of LTG on Ih reported in neurons are likely the result of indirect regulation, perhaps secondary to Na+ channel block.
source: These results clearly show that LTG is not a direct activator of HCN channels and suggest that any effects reported in neurons are the result of indirect regulation of Ih, perhaps secondary to Na+ channel block, and likely contingent on cell-specific, state-dependent signal transduction pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The effects of LTG on Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals are likely due to its action to directly block Na+ channels rather than an enhancement of HCN currents.
source: Although further experiments in mouse brain slices are needed to fully rule out an effect of this drug on native HCN channels with pathogenic sequence variants, it seems likely the effects of LTG on Hcn1GD/+ and Hcn1MI/+ animals are due to its action to directly block Na+ channels – similar to the effects of phenytoin – rather than an enhancement of HCN currents.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Compared to the effect of ZD7288 to reduce the current expressed by WT HCN1 channels by approximately 67%, the drug was minimally effective in blocking either the instantaneous or the time-dependent current component generated by mutant WT/G391D channels (approximately 15% inhibition).
source: As illustrated in Figure 10A and B, compared to the effect of ZD7288 to reduce the current expressed by WT HCN1 channels by ~67%, the drug was minimally effective in blocking either the instantaneous or the time-dependent current component generated by mutant WT/G391D channels (~15% inhibition).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from heterologous expression experiments, supported by data in Figure 10A and B.

claim: Addition of Cs+ led to a strong reduction in the current expressed by both WT and G391D channels.
source: Addition of Cs+, another HCN channel blocker (albeit a less specific one, compared to ZD7288) with a different mechanism of action and binding site (DiFrancesco, 1982), led to a strong reduction in the current expressed by both WT and G391D channels (Figure 10A), confirming that the observed currents were indeed generated by HCN1 WT/G391D heteromeric channels.
evidence: This is a control experiment result, supported by data in Figure 10A and a citation.

claim: Application of ZD7288 did not modify either the RMP or input resistance in Hcn1GD/+ neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 10C–E, application of the compound did not modify either the RMP or input resistance in Hcn1GD/+ neurons, while appropriately eliminating voltage sag, hyperpolarizing the RMP, and increasing input resistance in WT neurons.
evidence: This is a direct observation from brain slice electrophysiology experiments, supported by data in Figure 10C-E.

claim: ZD7288 appropriately eliminated voltage sag, hyperpolarized the RMP, and increased input resistance in WT neurons.
source: As shown in Figure 10C–E, application of the compound did not modify either the RMP or input resistance in Hcn1GD/+ neurons, while appropriately eliminating voltage sag, hyperpolarizing the RMP, and increasing input resistance in WT neurons.
evidence: This is a direct observation from brain slice electrophysiology experiments, supported by data in Figure 10C-E.
